title: Vitamin D Supplementation in Pregnancy and Lactation and Infant Growth
authors: Roth DE, Morris SK, Zlotkin S, Gernand AD, Ahmed T, Shanta SS, et al.
followUp: from 17 to 24 weeks of gestation to 1 year of infant age
population: Generally healthy pregnant women in Dhaka, Bangladesh; 64% were vitamin D deficient (25-hydroxyvitamin D below 30 nmol/L) at enrolment
funder: Funded by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (OPP1066764). The trial funder had no role in trial design, data collection, analysis or interpretation of the results.
inKindSupport: Vitamin D3 and placebo tablets were manufactured by the Toronto Institute for Pharmaceutical Technology.
authorConflicts: Disclosure forms available with the full text at NEJM.org; not read.
result: Five groups: placebo; 4200, 16,800 or 28,000 IU/week prenatally with placebo postpartum; or 28,000 IU/week prenatally and for 26 weeks postpartum. Among 1164 infants assessed at one year (90% of 1300 pregnancies), length-for-age z-scores did not differ (-0.93, -1.11, -0.97, -1.06 and -0.94; P=0.23), nor did other anthropometric measures, birth outcomes or morbidity. Confirmed hypercalcaemia, all asymptomatic, occurred in no women prenatally, 8 women (0.7%) postpartum (5 in the prenatal-and-postpartum group) and 6 infants (0.7%), without significant differences between groups; the risk of possible maternal hypercalciuria at delivery rose with dose; no women had urinary tract stones. A correction notice was published in 2021 (N Engl J Med 385:1728).
